title: Does 5% TEA Treatment of Red Film make it Green Sensitive

posts.topic_title: Does 5% TEA Treatment of Red Film make it Green Sensitive
posts.author: John Sonley
posts.post_subject: Does 5% TEA Treatment of Red Film make it Green Sensitive
posts.content_md:
I recently treated some Ilford red sensitive holography film with 5% TEA to speed it up and after some unusual results tried developing a piece of unexposed film, which blackened-up very quickly in Pyrochrome developer.

As the TEA treatment was done under the light of my dim green safelight I'm wondering how the film became fogged; could it be that the TEA treatment causes the red film to also be sensitive to green light.

The safelight has been in use for 20 years and I've never experiencede problems before

posts.topic_title: Does 5% TEA Treatment of Red Film make it Green Sensitive
posts.author: Ed Wesly
posts.post_subject: Does 5% TEA Treatment of Red Film make it Green Sensitive
posts.content_md:
It didn’t necessarily make it sensitive to green, it just made it more sensitive, enough to fog under your safelights.

Michael Wenyon showed me something that I had long suspected, that there is a special safelight for the Agfa products. If you look at the Spectral Sensitivity Curve for 8E75HD, (for instance go to [http://nlutie.com/ewesly/GP61.html](http://nlutie.com/ewesly/GP61.html) and click on Agfa Gevaert Technical Information Bulletin 21.7271(480)) you will see that there is considerable green sensitivity, with a dip at approximately 500 nm. Michael had a safelight filter, he called it V502, a narrow band green filter for that Agfa’s notch.

My own experience has proven to me that a lot of the so-called red holographic emulsions, Agfa, current Harman, do have green sensitivity. In fact, Agfa 10E75 is just about as sensitive at 532 as at 633 nm! And you can see that on the chart.

Traditionally in photography the Kodak No. 3 Safelight Filter was used to look at panchromatic films mid-development. (A Wratten No. 3 is a different animal.) It too, has a notch close to the dip of the Agfa red-sesitizing dye. [http://www.kodak.com/global/en/professi ... ti0845.pdf](http://www.kodak.com/global/en/professional/support/techPubs/ti0845/ti0845.pdf)

Its green color was adopted not because of the film’s sensitivity, but the human eye’s, whose peak sensitivity is in the green.

So your safelights may have tested out fine in the past, but in light of the fact that the TEA does make the film 2 to 4 times more sensitive, so you may have gotten over a threshold of exposure with the doping. Try going darker.

Another possibility is that the film was fogged before you started with the TEA. Although I am sure you have checked that also.

Since TEA is colorless, it should have no effect as a color sensitizer, as they need to be color complementary to the wavelength pursued; viz. the cyan color of the dye in the red sensitive emulsions. TEA is just as an overall sensitizer.

Recently Hans Bjelkhagen confirmed something about the old Ilford holographic plates (as compared to the current production of Harman Technology Ilford) that I had also suspected; that they bought from Agfa the cyan dye that makes the holographic film sensitive to the NIR, especially for the edge of human eye sensitivity 694 nm wavelength of the Ruby laser. It might have been part of the deal to keep the prices of both the products almost exactly the same.

The usual panchromatic dyes for photographic film take a nose dive before 700 nm, so Agfa came out with a dye that extended the response out to 750 nm (which explains the 75 in the film’s nomenclature) and I had found that it even worked further in the IR with a 780 nm diode laser. It must be a difficult chemical engineering problem to solve, as there are only a few photographic emulsions that cross the visible spectrum barrier, such as this one, which I suspect use this dye. [http://www.freestylephoto.biz/pdf/IlfordSFX200.pdf](http://www.freestylephoto.biz/pdf/IlfordSFX200.pdf) And I also suspect that the dye might be produced by Agfa, itself a word which doesn’t trip too easily off the tip of the tongue, but is a merciful abbreviation for Aktiengesellschaft für Anilinfabrikation, Corporation for Aniline (Dye) production, which is what they had started producing in the 19th century.

Maybe it’s time to invest in some Infrared Emitting Diodes and night vision goggles!

posts.content_md:
Ed - thank you for your very detailed reply.

I've checked back in my library and have a copy of that early Agfa spec. sheet - and sure enough the 8E75 HD film is sensitive into the wavelenghts approaching green.

The Ilford film in its box hasn't been fogged by an earlier exposure as my 1st test with it caused me to think that something was wrong as it required about 120mJ/cm -2 to blacken-up upon development - that's why I ventured towards TEA treatment; my normal Agfa film needs 20 - 30 mJ.

Thinking about it though - the process of cutting the large sheets of film (16" X12") into 5" X 4" pieces, soaking in 5% TEA, rubber blading (squeegeeing) and then drying with a hair dryer v. slowly, stacking between paper separators and finally boxing up ................ all takes time under the green safelight

I guess I'm looking for a piece of filter that lets through just circa 490nm - can anyone oblige?

Thanks Ed

> **Martin:** (how come that small companies like Slavich, HRT/Colourholographics, Ultimate were/are able to produce far better quality materials?!)

Possibly because they were made or designed by holographers? I believe Stas is responsible for Slavich, Gentet for Ultimate, Birdenheide and Inyake (Birkenheide? sorry, I don't know their exact names, I think they sounds something like this.) for Colourholographics. The large manufacturers, such as Kodak etc, seem to have simply transferred their production units into what they believed was the requirement for holographic film. I do remember that the Fuji guy who cam to our lab with a sample to test told me that the production units were not being used to full capacity because very few people used film anymore, so they simply "switched" to holography (whatever "switched" means!). Apparently also the fact that Fuji was pan was simply because they're production units were designed to make colour film. I had an interesting experience once when I was at one of our booths at a trade show. Someone who had been a photographer for 30 years asked me about holography. I explained that the film was very similar to photography but that it was of a higher density, so it needed special developers. He asked me what the special developers were. I asked him if he knew about developers. He got a little angry and said, "I've been in photography for 30 years! I think I know all about developers!". So, I said, "OK, well we use mainly metol ascorbic acid developers. The developer I use is based on Pyrocatechol" He then said, "I don't know what actually goes into the developer. I just know them by the name on the box"!

Stas only distributes the Slavich products through GEOLA. A guy named Suzanov, forgot first name, was the man in charge of holographic production at Slavich.

(Here’s an interesting anecdote about him. At the 1997 ISDH, he took a fancy to a woman from Portugal. His English was non-existent, hers sort of, but he still wanted her to come back to his room. So he spoke in Russian to my Russian girlfriend, who translated it into English, for Jesus Lopez to communicate to the object of Suzanov’s affections in Spanish, which I guess is close enough to Portuguese for pillow talk. The conversation broke down after a round or two.)

The original Holographic Recording Technology, HRT, plates were called BB for Biehrenheidt and Blyth; Colour Holographics took the BB out and replaced it with CH.

Suzanov moved on from Slavich, many peple say that’s why Slavich sucks, because the mastermind is gone. He started his own company, Sphere-S, which makes some of the best plates I have ever used, which GEOLA distributes, but is not on their web site, the GEO-3 panchromatic series.

You are right about Yves Gentet producing the Ultimate series, and I have to agree that they are the Ultimate! (Tied with GEO-3, see details forthcoming on my web site.)

It’s a good thing we have a forum like this to set the record straight! Only 1 out of 3 suppositions correct!

posts.content_md:
Fair enough. But, do holographers make these films? Are all the people you mention holographers? I don't know this Suzanov, but it sounds like he moves in holographic circles. Certainly Blyth and Gentet are holographers. My point was in answer to Martin's query as to how the smaller producers of holographic filsm were so much better than the Kodak's and the Fuji's. My belief, perhaps incorrect, is that holographers know about holographic emulsions more than the big film producers do. So, true, I don't know who made Slavich, hence my stateemnt about the fact I believe that Stas made it. I did know about Biehrenheidt, it's just that I didn't know how to spell it and so spelt it "Birdenheide". In fact I had several conversations with Vinteq about it and Rob Mundy told me some things about Biehrenheidt also. According to Vinteq, Biehrenheidt simply got tired and didn't want to produce the film since he figured that he was never going to get rich handmaking film in his basement, so he was glad to pass it on to Mike Midori. Now, note, this is second hand from Vinteq, so I can't swear to the legitimacy of the story - I simply pass it on for what it's worth. My bailiwick is the physics, optics and mathematics of holography.

For me, the fact that Colourholographics does not produce the BB Pan is the greater tragedy (Mike sent me an email stating that they were no longer making it for sale.) BB Pan is the only film I've used that makes decent colour holograms. I've heard good things about Ultimate, but it's a bit pricey just for research.
